q: Arrange NH₃, CH₃NH₂ and C₆H₅NH₂ in order of decreasing basicity in water.
x: The electron-donating CH₃ group pushes electron density onto N, so methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia. In phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is the weakest base. Putting phenylamine above ammonia ignores this delocalisation.

q: The amine (CH₃)₃C–NH₂ is classified as:
x: Amines are classified by the number of carbon groups on the nitrogen. Here N carries one alkyl group and two H atoms, so it is primary. Calling it tertiary confuses this with alcohols, which are classified by the carbon atom (here a tertiary carbon).

q: Propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN, is reduced with LiAlH₄ in dry ether. The product is:
x: Reduction adds 4 H to the C≡N group: R–C≡N + 4[H] → R–CH₂NH₂, keeping all three carbon atoms, so propan-1-amine forms. Ethylamine wrongly loses the nitrile carbon; the amide and the acid come from hydrolysis, not reduction.

q: Ethanenitrile, CH₃CN, is boiled under reflux with excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The organic product is:
x: Acid hydrolysis converts –C≡N, through the amide, into –COOH: CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl. Ethylamine is the product of reduction, not hydrolysis.

q: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is heated with phosphorus(V) oxide. The organic product is:
x: Phosphorus(V) oxide is a dehydrating agent and removes H₂O from the amide: CH₃CONH₂ → CH₃C≡N + H₂O. Ethylamine would need reduction with LiAlH₄, and methylamine would need Br₂ and NaOH (Hofmann reaction).

q: Bromoethane is heated with ammonia in ethanol in a sealed tube. Which condition makes ethylamine, rather than more substituted amines, the main product?
o: Water in place of ethanol as the solvent
Adding concentrated H₂SO₄ to the mixture
x: Ethylamine is itself a nucleophile and reacts with more bromoethane to give secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary salt. With a large excess of NH₃, bromoethane is far more likely to meet ammonia. Excess bromoethane favours the quaternary salt, and acid would protonate NH₃ so it is no longer a nucleophile.

q: Phenylamine is treated with NaNO₂ and dilute HCl below 5 °C, and the solution is then warmed. The organic product and the gas given off are:
x: Below 5 °C phenylamine forms benzenediazonium chloride, C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻. On warming in water it decomposes: C₆H₅N₂⁺ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + N₂ + H⁺. Chlorobenzene would need CuCl (Sandmeyer reaction), and the gas is nitrogen, not NO₂.

q: Phenylamine is shaken with excess bromine water at room temperature. The white precipitate formed is:
x: The –NH₂ group strongly activates the ring and directs to the 2-, 4- and 6-positions, so all three are substituted without a catalyst, as with phenol. Choosing only the 4-bromo product underestimates this activation; the 3- and 5-positions are meta and are not favoured.

q: Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, is a much weaker base than ethylamine, CH₃CH₂NH₂, because in ethanamide:
o: The nitrogen atom has no lone pair
The molecule is too large to accept a proton
The nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the C=O group
The C=O group donates electrons to the nitrogen
x: In an amide the N lone pair overlaps with the π bond of C=O (resonance), so it is far less available to accept H⁺ and amides are almost neutral. The C=O group withdraws electron density rather than donating it, and the amide nitrogen still has its lone pair.

q: How many amines (primary, secondary and tertiary together) have the molecular formula C₃H₉N?
x: Primary: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ and (CH₃)₂CHNH₂; secondary: CH₃NHCH₂CH₃; tertiary: (CH₃)₃N. That makes 4. Counting only the primary amines gives 2, and missing the tertiary amine gives 3.

q: Which conditions convert ethanol mainly into ethanal?
o: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distilling the product off as it forms
x: Ethanal (b.p. about 21 °C) is distilled out before it can be oxidised further. Under reflux it stays in contact with the oxidant and becomes ethanoic acid. LiAlH₄ is a reducing agent, and hot concentrated H₂SO₄ dehydrates ethanol to ethene.

q: Which reagent lengthens the carbon chain of a halogenoalkane by one carbon atom?
x: CN⁻ replaces the halogen and brings in the nitrile carbon: CH₃CH₂Br + KCN → CH₃CH₂CN + KBr. The other reagents give an alcohol, an amine or an alkene with the same number of carbon atoms.

q: Which three-step sequence converts ethanol into propanoic acid?
o: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇; then KCN in ethanol; then heat with dilute HCl
PBr₃; then KCN in ethanol; then heat with dilute HCl
PBr₃; then aqueous NaOH; then acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
PBr₃; then NH₃ in ethanol; then heat with dilute HCl
x: Ethanol → bromoethane (PBr₃) → propanenitrile (CN⁻ adds a carbon) → propanoic acid (acid hydrolysis of –CN). Oxidising first gives ethanoic acid, which does not form a nitrile with KCN; going back through ethanol and oxidising gives ethanoic acid with only two carbons.

q: Which Grignard reagent and carbonyl compound give propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, after hydrolysis with dilute acid?
x: The alkyl group of RMgBr bonds to the carbonyl carbon: CH₃ + CH₃CHO gives (CH₃)₂CHOH, a secondary alcohol with three carbons. Methanal gives the primary propan-1-ol, propanone gives the tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol, and C₂H₅MgBr with ethanal gives butan-2-ol.

q: Which reagent converts propanoic acid into propanoyl chloride?
x: Thionyl chloride replaces the –OH of the acid by –Cl: CH₃CH₂COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃CH₂COCl + SO₂ + HCl (PCl₅ also works). HCl cannot do this, and Cl₂ in sunlight substitutes hydrogen atoms on the alkyl chain.

q: Nitrobenzene is converted into phenylamine by:
o: Heating with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄
Heating with Sn and concentrated HCl, then adding NaOH
x: Sn/HCl reduces –NO₂ to –NH₂; the amine first forms as its salt, C₆H₅NH₃⁺, and NaOH releases free phenylamine. Concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ would nitrate the ring further, and KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent, the opposite of what is needed.

q: To prepare 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene from benzene, the best method is:
o: Brominate with Br₂/FeBr₃ first, then nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄
Nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄ first, then brominate with Br₂/FeBr₃
Nitrate and brominate together in one step with Br₂ and HNO₃
Treat with Br₂ in sunlight first, then nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄
x: –NO₂ is a meta director, so bromination after nitration puts Br at position 3. Brominating first gives mainly the 2- and 4-nitro products, because –Br is an ortho/para director. Br₂ in sunlight adds to benzene instead of substituting it.

q: Propan-1-ol is heated with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C to give X. X then reacts with HBr in the absence of peroxide to give Y. Y is:
x: Dehydration gives propene, CH₃CH=CH₂. HBr adds by Markovnikov's rule, H to the CH₂ carbon and Br to the middle carbon, giving CH₃CHBrCH₃. 1-Bromopropane is the anti-Markovnikov product, which needs peroxide.

q: Ethene is converted into ethane-1,2-diol in one step by:
x: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent) adds two –OH groups across the C=C bond. Hot acidified KMnO₄ breaks the C=C bond completely, steam gives ethanol, and bromine water gives brominated products.

q: Ethyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃, is best made by heating which pair with a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄?
x: In the ester name, 'ethyl' comes from the alcohol and 'propanoate' from the acid. Ethanoic acid with propan-1-ol gives the isomer propyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃, which is the tempting slip.
